claims.text: Single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticle formation is mainly governed by the interplay between rapid reduction/nucleation and limited atomic diffusion.
Rapid heating and cooling kinetically trap atoms in a non-equilibrium single-phase solid solution.
Allowing more time for atomic diffusion during cooling permits surface-energy differences to drive phase separation or structural reordering.
Slower cooling at an unchanged rapid heating rate extends the time available for post-reduction atomic diffusion.
Rapid thermal processing typically produces kinetically trapped, single-phase noble-metal HEA nanoparticles.
Post-nucleation atomic diffusion, particularly near emerging grain boundaries, is the structural mediator affected by cooling rate.
Rapid heating causes fast precursor reduction and nucleation.
Limited diffusion during rapid cooling prevents atoms from rearranging into lower-energy configurations.
Lower-energy atomic configurations may involve phase separation or elemental segregation.
Slower cooling provides sufficient diffusion for interfacial- and surface-energy minimization to produce phase-separated regions or distinct structural order.
Slower cooling will increase the incidence of secondary phases, mixed-phase structures, or crystallographic reordering relative to rapid cooling.
The rapid-heating and rapid-cooling baseline typically yields a single-phase, kinetically trapped solid solution.
The proposed mechanism applies to nanoparticles containing more than five noble-metal elements under rapid thermal processing.
Large differences in elemental size or binding energy may cause factors other than kinetic trapping to dominate structure selection.
Atomic-size differences and mixing enthalpies may alter diffusion rates and phase evolution across alloy compositions.
A lack of observable phase separation, enhanced ordering, or significant crystal-structure change under slower cooling would falsify kinetic trapping by rapid cooling as the governing mechanism.
